name: Hume's total scepticism and his retreat into 'natural credulity'
plain_explanation: Having argued that no belief -- not even belief in cause and effect, an external world, or the continuity of the self -- can be rationally justified, Hume doesn't conclude we should stop believing these things. Instead, he says nature simply forces us to believe them anyway, whether or not reason can back them up; the only 'remedy' for his own sceptical doubts is 'carelessness and inattention.'
precise_definition: Hume concludes 'all probable reasoning is nothing but a species of sensation,' and that belief is 'more properly an act of the sensitive, than of the cogitative part of our natures'; he does not refute his own sceptical arguments but instead falls back on the claim that 'nature, by an absolute and uncontrollable necessity has determined us to judge as well as to breathe and feel,' recommending 'carelessness and inattention' as the only practical remedy for total scepticism.
why_it_mattered: Russell treats this as 'the bankruptcy of eighteenth-century reasonableness': Hume set out, in the spirit of Locke, to be purely sensible and empirical, but his superior rigor led him to the 'disastrous conclusion that from experience and observation nothing is to be learnt' -- and Russell judges Hume's practical abandonment of his own scepticism to be, in a sense, 'insincere,' since he cannot actually live by it.
historical_origin: Book I, Part IV, Sections I and II of the Treatise ('Of scepticism with regard to reason' and 'Of scepticism with regard to the senses').
examples: Hume's own 'funeral oration' describing his mild, cheerful temperament, which Russell contrasts with the destructive implications of his philosophy
Hume's admission that he continues to believe fire warms and water refreshes only because 'it costs us too much pains to think otherwise'
objections: Russell's charge of inconsistency: in the later, non-sceptical portions of the Treatise, Hume 'forgets all about his fundamental doubts' and writes like any other Enlightenment moralist, applying to himself the very 'carelessness and inattention' he elsewhere prescribes as a philosophical remedy

Russell notes Hume has no right, on his own principles, to call anything 'dangerous' (a causal word) once he has undermined rational belief in causation, yet Hume does call the errors of religion 'dangerous'
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell argues this self-refutation of Enlightenment rationality was 'inevitably ... followed by a great outburst of irrational faith,' symbolized by Hume's quarrel with the emotionally volatile Rousseau, and feeding into nineteenth- and twentieth-century currents of 'unreason.'
